references.text: Naaman, the Syrian army commander – a foreigner – returned to give glory to the God of Israel after being healed of leprosy ([ref:2 Kings 5:15|2 Kings 5:15]). This account is a strong parallel to the Samaritan leper who returned to thank God.

The prophet Isaiah speaks about foreigners (outsiders) who attach themselves to the Lord, saying they will be welcomed into God's house ([ref:Isaiah 56:6-7|Isaiah 56:6-7]). This emphasizes that even "the foreigner" can give glory to God and be accepted.

Jesus himself referred to Naaman the Syrian's healing as an example of how God's grace went to foreigners rather than Israelites ([ref:Luke 4:27|Luke 4:27]). This is thematically closely linked to the fact that it was only the Samaritan outsider who returned to give thanks.

In the parable of the Good Samaritan, once again a Samaritan acts righteously, in contrast to the religious leaders ([ref:Luke 10:33|Luke 10:33]). Luke repeatedly highlights that Samaritans show faith and gratitude.

The hostility between Jews and Samaritans is illuminated in [ref:John 4:9|John 4:9], where it is explained that Jews had no dealings with Samaritans. This provides background for the startling fact that it was precisely "this foreigner" (ἀλλογενής) who returned.

The immediate context shows that it was the Samaritan who returned, fell on his face at Jesus' feet, and thanked him ([ref:Luke 17:15-16|Luke 17:15-16]). Verse 18 is Jesus' rhetorical comment that only this one – the foreigner – came back to give God glory.

The psalmist urges offering thanksgiving to God ([ref:Psalm 50:14|Psalm 50:14]). The nine who were healed but did not return neglected precisely this – giving God glory and thanks – which makes the Samaritan's response all the more remarkable.

In [ref:Acts 8:5-8|Acts 8:5-8], the Samaritans receive the gospel with joy. This confirms the pattern already hinted at in Luke 17:18 – that those regarded as foreigners proved receptive to God's work.
Paul writes that Gentiles should praise God for his mercy ([ref:Romans 15:9|Romans 15:9]). The Samaritan leper who gives glory to God is an early example of "foreigners" praising God for his grace.
